claims.claim: The working definition of a team in this lesson follows Katzenbach and Smith (Harvard Business Review, 'The Discipline of Teams') as presented in OpenStax's Principles of Management: a team is a group of people with complementary skills working toward a shared goal with mutual accountability; OpenStax lists the five functioning elements as common commitment and purpose, specific performance goals, complementary skills, commitment to how the work gets done, and mutual accountability.

Teams differ from working groups: a working group has a focused leader, individual accountabilities and individual work products, and its performance is a function of what members do as individuals, while a team has shared leadership, both individual and mutual accountability, and collective work products; Katzenbach and Smith add that when a task does not demand joint work-products, a working group can be the more effective option.

Organizations use teams because complex work needs many hands and minds: OpenStax opens its teams chapter with the idea that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts (a saying credited to Aristotle), and OpenStax's Introduction to Business states that pooling the skills and abilities of various specialists increases creativity and innovation and allows companies to tackle more complex tasks.

The three common team types are functional teams (members from the same department or function doing that department's work), cross-functional teams (members from different functions working on one shared project — the pattern of matrix structures, which bring people from different functional areas together for a special project), and self-managed teams (teams that organize their own work, such as the self-directed work teams OpenStax describes in manufacturing).

What makes teams work: a clear goal and direction (Katzenbach and Smith: establish urgency, demanding performance standards, and direction); roles (select members for their skill and skill potential; role clarity among the collaboration factors in the Gratton and Erickson research OpenStax cites); trust (time spent together builds camaraderie and trust; Lencioni's first dysfunction is absence of trust, which produces fear of conflict); and communication (clear rules of behavior, fresh facts, and positive feedback).

Teams carry honest costs: coordination takes time (teams need rules of behavior, time together, and agreement on how the work gets done, and a manager quoted in OpenStax says building an environment for teamwork takes time), and conflict happens (OpenStax lists communication breakdowns, competing views or goals, power struggles, and personality conflicts as sources, with poorly handled conflict creating distrust and disrupting progress and morale).

Team cohesion — the strength and extent of interpersonal connection among the members of a group — keeps members motivated to accomplish the team's goals; CFI defines cohesive teams as having an attitude of 'we-ness' and lists shared goals, time spent together, and previous successes among the influences on cohesion.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which team types a taxonomy should name
positions: Different management texts sort teams differently: Robbins-style texts often list problem-solving teams, self-managed teams, cross-functional teams, and virtual teams, while other texts emphasize functional teams.

This lesson names three types — functional, cross-functional, and self-managed — as the common shapes, each grounded in verified OpenStax material (working groups organized by functional area; matrix structures joining different functional areas for a project; self-directed work teams in manufacturing).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: No substantive conflict: the lesson presents the three types as common shapes rather than an exhaustive catalog, grounds each type in OpenStax, and explicitly notes that organizations also form temporary project teams and virtual teams as needed.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Business, Section 7.2: Contemporary Structures
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook; id reused from the phase-2 source registry with an identical URL). Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports: the matrix structure brings together people from different functional areas of the organization (such as manufacturing, finance, and marketing) to work on a special project; advantages include teamwork — pooling the skills and abilities of various specialists increases creativity and innovation and lets the company tackle more complex tasks — and higher performance through ownership and commitment; disadvantages include team members from different functional areas having difficulty communicating effectively and working together. Grounds the cross-functional team type and the many-hands-and-minds argument; content paraphrased into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: The Discipline of Teams (Katzenbach, J. R., & Smith, D. K., Harvard Business Review, March 1993)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier C (primary scholarly/business article; the canonical source of the working definition). hbr.org blocks direct fetching; verified via Wayback Machine capture web.archive.org/web/20140503204829/ on 2026-08-22. Supports: with a run-of-the-mill working group, performance is a function of what the members do as individuals, while a team's performance calls for both individual and mutual accountability; the essential discipline of five characteristics (meaningful common purpose, specific performance goals, a mix of complementary skills, commitment to how the work gets done, mutual accountability); if a task does not demand joint work-products, a working group can be the more effective option. Elements restated in original prose; no text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Team Cohesion — What It Is and Strategies to Develop It
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (finance education reference). Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports: team cohesion as the strength and extent of interpersonal connection existing among the members of a group; the interpersonal bond causes members to participate readily and remain motivated to accomplish the set goals; cohesive teams have an attitude of 'we-ness'; influences on cohesion include similarity of attitudes and values, size of the group, time, previous successes and shared goals, and threat and competition. Corroborates the interpersonal-bond dimension of what makes teams work; content paraphrased, no text reproduced.
